beyond_behavioral_benchmarks.title: Beyond Behavioral Benchmarks - Mechanistic Evaluation of LLM Demographic Encoding
beyond_behavioral_benchmarks.description: Carlos's working paper presents a four-phase mechanistic evaluation pipeline that audits how language models internally encode demographic identity, and whether those internal representations actually drive what the models say. The headline finding: behavioral output and internal representation can be substantially decoupled. A model can pass every fairness benchmark while internally computing demographic information in ways those benchmarks cannot detect, and in some cases while that internal information is doing nothing at all.
beyond_behavioral_benchmarks.the_question: When researchers use a language model to simulate how a Hispanic respondent might answer a survey question (a practice called silicon sampling), they assume the model is reaching for an internal representation of 'Hispanic' and reasoning from there. That assumption had never been tested mechanistically. So Carlos tested it.

methodology.summary: A four-phase mechanistic pipeline run across eight open-weights language models, from GPT-2 (117M) to Pythia-12B.
phases: Behavioral baseline: Run the BBQ fairness benchmark and record what the model says
Activation probing: Train a linear classifier on internal activations to test whether demographic identity is encoded

Causal patching: Surgically swap one demographic representation for another inside the residual stream and measure whether the output changes (this is the test for whether the encoding actually drives anything)
Semantic characterization: Project demographic encoding directions onto the model's vocabulary to surface representational artifacts invisible to behavioral evaluation
methodology.validation: Phases 1 through 3 produce statistically validated findings, permutation-tested with 1,000 iterations. Phase 4 is exploratory and model-specific.

key_findings: Demographic identity is encoded everywhere, all the time. A simple linear probe recovers race/ethnicity and gender at 100% accuracy from internal activations at every layer in every model tested. The encoding is concept-level, not token-specific (it survives paraphrasing 'Latino' for 'Hispanic').

Whether the encoding drives outputs depends on training. In base models like GPT-2 and Pythia-1.4B, the demographic encoding is causally active at intermediate layers but goes inert at the final layer (where behavioral evaluation looks). In Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1 the encoding is geometrically perfect (100% probe accuracy) but causally disconnected from every layer of computation. Instruction tuning restored behavioral sensitivity through a mechanism that operates entirely independently of the demographic encoding direction.

The encodings carry pretraining artifacts that no behavioral benchmark can see. In GPT-2, the Hispanic encoding direction loads on criminalization-adjacent vocabulary (detention, joints) when contrasted with White, and on Spanish surnames (Gomez, Cruz) when contrasted with Black. The Black encoding is dominated by color-compound subword tokens (Berry, jack, smith for Blackberry, Blackjack, Blacksmith) at early layers before shifting to civic vocabulary at later layers.
beyond_behavioral_benchmarks.why_it_matters: If you publish silicon-sampling results and validated your model on behavioral fairness benchmarks, that validation is not enough. The model can show clean behavioral output while drawing on representations shaped by criminalization associations or majority-context dependence. Geometric presence (what a probe measures), causal activity (what patching measures), and behavioral expression (what benchmarks measure) are three distinct properties that can diverge. Treating any one as a proxy for the others produces conclusions the evidence does not support.
what_next: Replicate findings on closed frontier models (GPT-4, Claude, Llama-3)
Sparse autoencoder decomposition of demographic encoding directions
Trace causal connection between intermediate-layer activity and final-layer outputs
Open-ended generation benchmarks (BOLD, HolisticBias) to test generalization beyond multiple-choice formats
Apply Phases 1-3 to models being used in published silicon-sampling studies

decision_coach.title: Decision Coach - A Dual-LLM Coaching System with Six-Dimension Assessment
decision_coach.description: Decision Coach (decisioncoach.io) is an AI-mediated coaching platform Carlos designed and deployed where users practice coaching an LLM persona through a real decision. The contribution that matters isn't the chat interface; it's the measurement instrument: a six-dimension Decision Quality rubric scored turn-by-turn by a separate LLM judge. Built around the principle that a coaching LLM should be designed not to answer.
decision_coach.the_question: Generic LLM chatbots haven't helped people make better decisions. They answer for users, replacing reasoning with instruction. What if you built a coaching system designed not to answer, an LLM whose pedagogy is restraint? And how would you measure whether it actually produced better decisions, when 'good decision' is famously slippery?

system_architecture.summary: Dual-LLM architecture with two agents in separate contexts, built around the measurement, not around the chat.
system_architecture.persona_llm: Jamie, a college sophomore navigating a major-switching decision. Has a backstory, an emotional state machine (confused, uncertain, thoughtful, confident), and cognitive constraints encoded in the system prompt. Jamie refuses to advance through the Decision Chain stages until the current dimension has been adequately covered. The refusal is the pedagogy.
system_architecture.evaluation_llm: Separate LLM that scores each user turn against the six-dimension Decision Quality rubric in a separate context, returning per-dimension scores and rationale.
system_architecture.session_design: 10-turn session limit transforms coaching from open-ended conversation into purposeful practice. Five personas shipped; one (Jamie) used in the pilot.
stack: Supabase Postgres with row-level security for participant data isolation
system_architecture.data_pipeline: IRB-compliant. Research-code pseudonymization with no PII in research exports.

measurement_instrument.framework: Decision Quality Science (Decision Education Foundation) six elements: Frame, Values, Alternatives, Information, Reasoning, Commitment.
measurement_instrument.scoring: Each user turn scored 0 to 1 on each dimension with behaviorally anchored levels. Aggregate is intentionally NOT a mean; it's the minimum across dimensions, the weakest link. A coaching session with strong framing but no commitment-to-action is incomplete, and a mean-based score would hide that.
measurement_instrument.calibration: Acceptable preliminary inter-rater reliability against expert practitioners (r = 0.71). Broader validation against multiple human annotators is ongoing.
measurement_instrument.why_automated: Turn-level human coding doesn't scale past about 50 sessions per study wave. The LLM evaluator replaces roughly 100 hours of human coding per wave, which is what makes the rest of the research design feasible.

decision_coach.reward_hacking_story: The technical anecdote that anchors the whole methodology came early. In the first version, Carlos used a single LLM instance to both generate Jamie's responses and score the user's turns. Scores looked excellent. When he split them into two separate LLM calls with separate prompts and separate contexts, average scores dropped about 0.10. That delta is the methodological argument for separation. A generator that also evaluates inflates its own scores. It's a textbook reward-hacking failure mode, and it's the moment Decision Coach became a research artifact rather than a demo.

pilot_results.design: IRB-approved pilot. 52 participants, 75 sessions, 68 with full turn-level scoring. College students, mixed undergrad and grad. Mean engagement: 11 turns per session.
pilot_results.headline: 91% of 68 sessions showed within-session improvement (+0.220 mean DQ, +151% relative). Mean DQ Overall went from 0.145 at first turn to 0.366 at last turn. 4% of sessions declined; 4% were unchanged.
pilot_results.caveat: This is within-session improvement, not a between-condition causal effect. The falsifiable test (not-knowing persona vs. all-knowing persona) is in the planned full study (target n approximately 200, between-subjects, with a 2 to 4 week longitudinal follow-up for skill transfer).
pilot_results.honest_research_note: Carlos's design hypothesis was that Commitment would be the weakest dimension at session-end. Per-dimension finals showed Alternatives is weakest (0.310), then Frame (0.334), Reasoning (0.356), Information (0.357), Commitment (0.381), Values (0.384). Binary thinking is the ceiling, not commitment. That's quantitative evaluation overturning a design assumption, which is exactly what a properly designed measurement instrument should do.

decision_coach.why_it_matters: The defensible contribution isn't the chat UI. It's the rubric plus LLM judge as a measurement instrument that scales beyond what human coding can support. The same instrument is, in principle, portable: it can evaluate human decision coaches, compare coaching approaches, or train practitioners. It operationalizes 'good judgment' into observable, scoreable behaviors. The system-level claim is more pointed: a coaching LLM that refuses to answer can produce measurable within-session learning.
what_next: Run the full study (n approximately 200, between-subjects: not-knowing vs. all-knowing persona, with mediation by user agency and moderation by educational level)
Longitudinal follow-up at 2 to 4 weeks to test whether coaching skills transfer to participants' own decisions
Comprehensive inter-rater reliability against multiple human annotators

Roll out the four additional personas (international students with visa constraints, returning adult students balancing education and family, students facing financial pressure, etc.) to test cross-scenario skill transfer

strategic_empathy.title: Strategic Empathy in Product Management
strategic_empathy.description: Redesigning APC roles in NM Scholars after realizing students felt invisible. Instead of scaling top-down, Carlos gave students relational power. This product decision was driven by deep understanding of user needs and business constraints.
strategic_empathy.situation: Students felt invisible in the NM Scholars program
strategic_empathy.approach: Redesigned APC roles to give students relational power and agency
strategic_empathy.principle: Instead of scaling top-down, empower users from within the system
strategic_empathy.business_impact: Increased student engagement and program retention

system_problems.title: Starting System Problems in Product Development
system_problems.description: Carlos identifies pain points, then maps who benefits from the status quo. Systems thinking begins with uncovering inertia and understanding the broader ecosystem in which products operate.
process: Identify user pain points and business opportunities
Map who benefits from the status quo
Uncover system inertia and resistance points
Design products that work within existing systems while creating transformation opportunities

competing_needs.title: Balancing Competing Stakeholder Needs
competing_needs.description: In NM Scholars, mentors wanted consistency while students needed flexibility. Carlos split the model: fixed templates, flexible timing. This product decision served both stakeholder groups while maintaining program integrity.
competing_needs.situation: Mentors wanted consistency, students needed flexibility
competing_needs.solution: Split the model: fixed templates, flexible timing
competing_needs.business_impact: Improved both mentor satisfaction and student engagement

scaling_ready.title: When a Product is Ready to Scale
scaling_ready.description: A product is ready to scale when it teaches without you, when its logic is modular, and when the values aren't diluted in translation. Carlos focuses on building products that can grow while maintaining their core value proposition.
criteria: When the product teaches users without direct involvement
When the product logic is modular and maintainable
When core values aren't diluted in translation to scale
When business metrics support sustainable growth

ai_vs_human.title: AI vs Human Judgment in Product Decisions
ai_vs_human.description: AI can generate options, summarize context, or prompt thinking. Judgment must always stay with humans—especially in identity-based work. Carlos designs AI products that amplify human capabilities rather than replace them.
ai_role: Prompt human thinking and decision making
ai_vs_human.human_role: Judgment must always stay with humans—especially in identity-based work and complex product decisions

immediate_vs_longterm.title: Immediate Needs vs Long-term Product Strategy
immediate_vs_longterm.description: Carlos designs scaffolds for today and templates for tomorrow. Tactical wins should support future transformation, not delay it. He balances immediate user needs with long-term business strategy.
approach: Design product scaffolds for immediate user needs
Create templates and frameworks for future transformation
Ensure tactical wins support long-term business strategy
Balance user satisfaction with sustainable business growth

vulnerable_users.title: Designing Products for Vulnerable Users
vulnerable_users.description: Carlos starts with their fears and barriers. Then he builds confidence through scaffolding, transparency, and reflection-based feedback loops. This approach not only serves ethical goals but also expands market reach.
process: Start with user fears and barriers
Create reflection-based feedback loops for continuous improvement
business_case: Serving vulnerable users expands market reach
Designing for edge cases improves overall product quality

misaligned_stakeholders.title: Handling Misaligned Stakeholders in Product Development
misaligned_stakeholders.description: Carlos maps stakeholder values, makes tensions visible, then facilitates reframing through mutual clarity rather than forced alignment. This approach creates products that serve multiple stakeholder needs simultaneously.
approach: Map stakeholder values and priorities
Make tensions and conflicts visible
Facilitate reframing through mutual clarity
Design products that serve multiple stakeholder needs
